prompt: Which of the four services is regional and reads every HTTP request?
hint: Regional and layer 7.

choices.text: Azure Load Balancer
choices.why: Regional, but layer 4: it reads addresses and ports, never a URL.

choices.text: Application Gateway
choices.why: Right. A reverse proxy in one region, deciding per request.

choices.text: Front Door
choices.why: It reads HTTP too, but it stands at the edge, in front of several regions.

choices.text: Traffic Manager
choices.why: It answers DNS queries and reads no request at all.

prompt: A user's browser was told by Traffic Manager to use endpoint A. Endpoint A fails a minute later. What does the user's next request do?
hint: Where was the decision made, and how long does it last?

choices.text: Traffic Manager reroutes it in flight to endpoint B
choices.why: No packet passes through Traffic Manager, so there is nothing in flight for it to reroute.

choices.text: It fails at once, and every later request fails as well
choices.why: Once the cache expires, the next lookup gets a healthy endpoint.

choices.text: It still goes to A until the cached answer expires
choices.why: Right. The decision lives in DNS, and DNS answers are cached for their TTL.

choices.text: Front Door takes over, since it backs up Traffic Manager
choices.why: They are separate services; neither stands behind the other unless you build it so.

prompt: The application behind an Application Gateway logs the source address of every request. What does it log?
hint: Who opened the connection the application received?

choices.text: The customer's own public address
choices.why: That is what a backend behind Load Balancer sees. A proxy opens a connection of its own.

choices.text: The address of Microsoft's nearest edge location
choices.why: Edge locations belong to Front Door, which this design does not have.

choices.text: Nothing, since a proxy strips the source address
choices.why: Every packet has a source; it is the gateway's.

choices.text: An address of the gateway, from its subnet
choices.why: Right. The customer's address arrives in `X-Forwarded-For` instead.

prompt: An Application Gateway keeps the customer's address in the ___ header.
hint: It starts with X.

prompt: Which of these can Application Gateway do and Load Balancer cannot? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which of them needs the request to be read?

choices.text: Send `/api/` to one pool and the pages to another
choices.why: Right. That needs the path, which only a layer 7 service reads.

choices.text: Spread UDP traffic across machines
choices.why: That is Load Balancer's work; the gateway handles HTTP.

choices.text: Host several sites on one address
choices.why: Right. It reads the host name in each request.

choices.text: Take health probes from the machines
choices.why: Both probe their backends; neither receives probes from them.

choices.text: Keep a user on one machine with a cookie
choices.why: Right. A cookie is part of the request, invisible at layer 4.

prompt: What happened to the Basic SKU of Azure Load Balancer?
hint: A date in September 2025.

choices.text: It was retired on 30 September 2025
choices.why: Right. Every load balancer created today is Standard.

choices.text: It was renamed Standard, with the same features
choices.why: Standard was a separate SKU with more features, not a new name.

choices.text: It moved to the global tier
choices.why: The global tier is a form of Standard, unrelated to Basic.

choices.text: It became the default for internal load balancers
choices.why: Internal ones are Standard too.

prompt: Match each list of `lb.bicep` to what it says.
hint: The rule is the one that joins the other three.

pairs.right: which port goes to which pool

right_distractors: which zone the load balancer sits in

prompt: The compiled template showed `"zones":null` for `lb-shop-web` and all three zones for `pip-shop-web`. What does that make the front end?
hint: Where does a Standard front end take its zones from?

choices.text: Zonal, in zone 1, since the load balancer named none
choices.why: Naming no zone does not mean zone 1. The front end follows its address.

choices.text: Invalid: a Standard load balancer must list its zones
choices.why: It compiled, and the load balancer resource has no zones property to fill.

choices.text: Zone-redundant, because its address spans the three
choices.why: Right. The load balancer itself is regional and has nothing to say about zones.

choices.text: Regional, with no protection against a zone failure
choices.why: The address is served from all three zones, so losing one does not take it down.

prompt: The shop's front end is zone-redundant, and all three web machines in `be-web` were created in zone 2. Zone 2 fails. What do customers get?
hint: Which half survived?

choices.text: Nothing: the address answers, and no machine behind it does
choices.why: Right. The front end survived a zone and the pool did not.

choices.text: The site, because the probe moves the machines to zone 1
choices.why: A probe only marks machines unfit. Nothing moves them.

choices.text: The site, served from the front end's copy in another zone
choices.why: A front end forwards traffic; it holds no copy of the site to serve.

choices.text: A redirect to the paired region, `southcentralus`
choices.why: A load balancer never sends traffic to another region on its own.

prompt: Why does `rule-https` set `disableOutboundSnat: true`?
hint: It is about connections the machines open, not the ones they receive.

choices.text: To stop customers from reaching the machines directly
choices.why: Inbound reach is the front end and the network's filters; this setting is about outbound.

choices.text: So outbound traffic takes a route of its own
choices.why: Right. A NAT gateway or an outbound rule, instead of running a shared address out of ports.

choices.text: Because HTTPS on port 443 cannot be translated
choices.why: Address translation works for any port; the reason is the shared address's ports.

choices.text: To keep each customer on one machine
choices.why: That is session persistence, a different setting the rule leaves at its default.

prompt: How does a web machine join the pool `be-web`?
hint: The pool in `lb.bicep` was left empty.

choices.text: By listing its name in the pool's `members` property
choices.why: The pool has no such list; it is filled from the other side.

choices.text: Automatically, by being in the same subnet
choices.why: Sharing a subnet puts nothing in a pool.

choices.text: By answering the probe for the first time
choices.why: The probe judges members; it does not enrol them.

choices.text: From its own network interface, which names the pool
choices.why: Right. Azure attaches a machine to a pool through its network interface.

prompt: `probe-http` asks every member for `/healthz` at a fixed interval. How many seconds is it?
hint: `intervalInSeconds`.

prompt: In the chain `dig` printed for `portal.azure.com`, which name belongs to Front Door?
hint: Look for the domain the lesson named for Front Door.

choices.text: `portal-prod-02-linkage.trafficmanager.net`
choices.why: `trafficmanager.net` is Traffic Manager, which decides first.

choices.text: `p-0010.p-msedge.net`
choices.why: That is one of the edge names at the end of the chain.

choices.text: `azureportal.z01.azurefd.net`
choices.why: Right. `azurefd.net` names a Front Door endpoint.

choices.text: `portal.azure.com`
choices.why: That is the name looked up, an alias for the rest.

prompt: Why did the lesson add `+nottlid` and `grep CNAME` to `dig`?
hint: What would differ between two runs?

choices.text: Because the addresses of Microsoft's services are secret
choices.why: They are public answers to anybody; they just vary by place and minute.

choices.text: To drop the TTLs and addresses, which change each time
choices.why: Right. What stays is the chain of names, which is the part worth reading.

choices.text: To stop `dig` from contacting Traffic Manager
choices.why: The query goes out the same way; the options only shape what is printed.

choices.text: Because `+nottlid` asks for the answer without caching
choices.why: It leaves the TTL out of the printout; the caches work as before.

prompt: `dig shop-azure-foundations-l22.trafficmanager.net` answered `NXDOMAIN`. What does that say?
hint: Whose zone is `trafficmanager.net`?

choices.text: Nobody has created a profile with that name
choices.why: Right. Names in `trafficmanager.net` are unique across Azure.

choices.text: The profile exists but is disabled
choices.why: A disabled profile still exists as a name. NXDOMAIN says there is none.

choices.text: The lab cannot reach Traffic Manager without an account
choices.why: It reached the DNS fine; the answer was that the name does not exist.

choices.text: Traffic Manager names cannot contain the digits `22`
choices.why: Digits are allowed; the name simply has no owner.

prompt: A multiplayer game sends UDP to servers in `brazilsouth` and `eastus` and wants each player on the nearer region. Which service fits?
hint: Ask the three questions in order.

choices.text: Front Door, with the latency routing of its origins
choices.why: Front Door proxies HTTP. UDP fails the first question.

choices.text: Application Gateway in each region
choices.why: Not HTTP, so not a layer 7 service, and each gateway sees one region.

choices.text: One internal Load Balancer spanning both regions
choices.why: An internal load balancer serves one region's network.

choices.text: Traffic Manager by performance, over a Load Balancer per region
choices.why: Right. DNS steering picks the region and layer 4 carries the UDP.

prompt: Why is Traffic Manager not in the shop's path to `shop.example`?
hint: Which service already chooses the region?

choices.text: Traffic Manager cannot point at a name in `brazilsouth`
choices.why: It can point at endpoints anywhere, Brazil included.

choices.text: It is retired, like the classic Front Door
choices.why: Traffic Manager is a current service. Classic is a tier of Front Door.

choices.text: Front Door already chooses the region
choices.why: Right. A second DNS layer would only add a cache to wait out.

choices.text: It costs more than Front Door for the same traffic
choices.why: The lesson quotes no price, and the reason given is about the design.

prompt: Put the stops of a customer's request in the shop's design in order, from the customer inwards.
hint: Global first, then regional, then between the tiers.
items: the nearest Front Door edge location
trap: Requests for `/api/` skip the web machines and go from the gateway to the application pool.

prompt: A team puts Traffic Manager with a 300-second TTL in front of two regions, and promises recovery "within a minute" of a region failing. What is wrong with the promise?
hint: Who holds the old answer, and for how long?

choices.text: Traffic Manager takes an hour to notice a failure
choices.why: Its probes notice in well under that. The delay is elsewhere.

choices.text: Traffic Manager cannot fail over between two regions
choices.why: Priority routing does exactly that.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as both regions are paired
choices.why: Pairing has no effect on how long DNS answers are cached.

choices.text: Cached answers keep users on the failed region up to five minutes
choices.why: Right. A 300-second TTL lets a resolver keep the old answer that long.

prompt: Match each need to the service the lesson's decision gives it.
hint: Layer first, then region.

pairs.left: TCP to a database tier in one region
HTTP in one region, `/api/` split from pages
HTTP in three regions, with an edge cache
any protocol, steered by DNS between regions

prompt: Which of these did the lab actually check about `lb.bicep`?
hint: What does a compiler know?

choices.text: That `brazilsouth` sells the Standard SKU
choices.why: That is a fact about Azure, known only at deployment.

choices.text: That its shape is one Azure accepts
choices.why: Right. Shape here, values there.

choices.text: That the public address is free in the region
choices.why: Addresses are handed out by Azure at deployment.

choices.text: That `/healthz` answers on the web machines
choices.why: No machine exists; the probe path is just a string.
